opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest difference is really about where your attention goes.

At a large company, like when I was at Facebook or Alibaba, you have an enormous amount of resources: compute, talent, infrastructure, and existing customers. The challenge there is more about alignment. You spend a lot of time making sure different teams are moving in the same direction, that priorities are clear, and that the thing you build fits into a much bigger picture. The scale lets you do things a small team simply can't, like running very large clusters or supporting a framework used across an entire company.

When you start a small company, almost everything flips. You don't have the resources, so every decision matters much more. You have to be very sharp about what problem you're solving and who you're solving it for, because you can't afford to build things nobody uses. The feedback loop is much shorter. You talk to a customer in the morning, and by the afternoon you may have changed your roadmap. That's very exciting, but also quite humbling.

Another big difference is that at a big company, a lot of things are taken care of for you: hiring pipelines, legal, sales, even the brand. As a founder, you suddenly realize how much work those things take. You end up being an engineer, a salesperson, a recruiter, sometimes even the person fixing the office printer. So you learn a lot, very quickly.

I wouldn't say one is better than the other. They're good for different stages and different goals. A large company is a great place to learn how systems work at scale and to see how technology gets deployed in the real world. A startup is where you test whether your own judgment about the future is actually right. For me, after many years in big companies, I felt AI infrastructure was changing so fast that a small, focused team could move faster and build something genuinely useful. That's what pulled me toward starting something of my own.

r001.rationale: The response says large companies spend time aligning teams, but does not identify business complexity as the reason extensive collaboration is needed.

r002.rationale: It says a small, focused team can move faster and describes a short customer feedback loop that can quickly change the roadmap.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the biggest difference is really about what you're optimizing for, and how close you are to the consequences of your own decisions.

At a large company, whether it was Google or Facebook or Alibaba, you have an enormous amount of leverage. When I worked on things like TensorFlow or PyTorch, the moment something shipped, it reached millions of developers. The infrastructure is there, the distribution is there, the people are there. You can focus on a very hard technical problem and trust that the rest of the machine will carry it. That's a wonderful thing, and I don't think people should underestimate how much you learn from seeing how a large system actually operates at scale.

But the flip side is that in a large company, a lot of the most important decisions are already made for you. The business model is set, the priorities come from above, and you're operating within a fairly well-defined box. Even at a senior level, you're often one input among many. Sometimes you see an opportunity very clearly and you still can't move toward it because it doesn't fit the company's direction that quarter.

When you start a small company, that box disappears. Nobody tells you what to do, which sounds liberating until you realize that also means nobody protects you from being wrong. Every decision, from what product to build to how to price it to who to hire, lands directly on you, and you feel the result very quickly. If customers don't want it, you know within weeks, not years. That tight feedback loop is painful but it's also the most honest teacher I've ever had.

The other thing I'd say is that at a big company, I spent most of my time thinking about technology. At a startup, I spend maybe a third of my time on technology, and the rest on customers, on the team, on cash, on things I never had to think about before. The technical problems are still there, but they're no longer the hardest problems. The hardest problems are figuring out what actually matters to someone who's going to pay you, and then building a team that can keep doing that over and over.

So I don't think one is better than the other. The large company teaches you how great systems are built. The small company teaches you why they need to exist in the first place. I'm glad I did them in that order.

r001.rationale: The response mentions large-company scale and decisions set by others, but does not identify business complexity or extensive cross-team collaboration as a reason.

r002.rationale: It says startups have fewer constraints and provide faster customer feedback, but does not clearly state that small companies have an advantage in quickly bringing an idea to reality.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest difference is how you deal with uncertainty. At a large company, you usually have a lot of resources and an established business. You may be working on a very difficult problem, but there’s a structure around it: teams, processes, and people with specialized expertise.

When you start a small company, you have to build that structure while also figuring out what’s worth doing. Who is the customer? What problem matters enough that they’ll pay for a solution? What should you do yourself, and when should you hire someone? Those questions are all connected, and you can’t wait until you have perfect information to make a decision.

The nice thing is that the feedback loop is much shorter. You talk to a customer, see something that needs to change, and you can change it immediately. But you also feel the consequences more directly. So I wouldn’t say one is simply harder than the other. A large company teaches you how to accomplish things at scale; a small company forces you to be very clear about what deserves your limited time and resources.

r001.rationale: The response mentions teams and processes at large companies, but does not say business complexity makes extensive cross-team collaboration necessary.

r002.rationale: It says a small company has a much shorter feedback loop and can make changes immediately, communicating an advantage over large companies when moving quickly.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest difference is how you deal with uncertainty. In a large company, you usually have a lot of resources, and the challenge is figuring out how to bring those resources together—getting people aligned, working across teams, and making sure an idea can have an impact at scale.

When you start a small company, you have much less support, but you can move very quickly. You can talk to a customer, learn that your assumption was wrong, and change direction that afternoon. The feedback is very direct. At the same time, you’re responsible for everything, including things you may never have thought about as an engineer.

So I wouldn’t say one is necessarily better. They teach you different things. A large company teaches you how to scale an effort. A startup forces you to ask whether you’re doing something people actually need, and whether you can deliver it before you run out of time and resources.

r001.rationale: The response mentions aligning people and working across teams at large companies, but does not identify business complexity as the reason extensive collaboration is needed.

r002.rationale: It says small companies can move very quickly and change direction that afternoon, contrasting this with the coordination and scale challenges at large companies.
